concept.title: The Loyalty Test Nobody Saw Coming
concept.core_idea: A long-term customer of a local service business casually drops a bombshell mid-conversation: they almost left — not because of the service, but because six weeks of silence on social made them assume the business had quietly shut down. The owner had no idea their feed going dark was being read as a closing sign.
concept.product_role: fenrik Studio is introduced at the resolution as the reason this conversation never has to happen again. The owner only needs a website URL — no brief, no camera, no content team. The first package is free. The point is not to sell a service; it is to remove the only thing standing between a busy business and a consistent social presence.
concept.why_it_works: The humor mode works here because the situation is absurdly recognizable — the business was thriving, and a loyal customer almost left because of a silent Instagram account. The joke is on the gap between reality and perception, not on the owner. The customer's delivery is deadpan and kind, which makes the punchline land harder. The POV is the customer's experience, which is fresh relative to recent fingerprints that stayed inside the owner's perspective. The proof point — first package free, website URL only — arrives at the exact moment the viewer is most receptive: right after the punchline makes the cost of inaction concrete and slightly funny.
concept.narrative_arc: SITUATION: A local plumbing business owner is having a perfectly normal catch-up chat with a customer he has known for four years. The customer mentions, almost as an aside, that he nearly called a competitor last month. The owner assumes it was a pricing thing, or maybe a scheduling issue — something fixable. He asks what happened. The customer shrugs and says he just figured they had closed. The owner blinks. Closed? They had their busiest quarter on record. UNEXPECTED TURN: The customer pulls out his phone, opens Instagram, and shows the owner his own profile — the last post is from seven weeks ago. He explains, without any drama, that he googled the business, the website looked fine, but the social feed was dead. No posts, no stories, nothing. In his mind, that meant something was wrong. He almost called someone else out of genuine concern, not disloyalty. PUNCHLINE: The owner stares at the phone. His business did not go quiet because anything was wrong. It went quiet because nobody had time to post. And it turns out, to a customer who could not call to check, quiet and closed look exactly the same. CTA: fenrik Studio is introduced as the fix — submit your website URL, get your first content package free, no camera or content team required.
concept.emotional_tone: Warm and lightly comedic — the humor comes from the absurdity of the situation, not from mocking anyone. The owner's reaction lands as instantly relatable. The customer is not upset, just honest. The punchline is a gentle gut-punch that makes the viewer laugh and wince at the same time.
concept.audience_insight: Local service businesses, small ecommerce brands, and solo operators often treat social media as optional when they are busy — precisely when they should be most visible. They do not realize that customers use social activity as a live signal of whether a business is still operating, healthy, and worth trusting. A quiet feed does not just look boring; to a customer who cannot see behind the scenes, it looks like a closed sign.

visual_direction.camera_style: Handheld with slight natural drift — feels observational, like someone nearby caught the moment. Close on faces during the conversation. Tight on the phone screen for the pivot. Pull back slightly on the punchline beat to let the owner's expression breathe.

package.title: The Loyalty Test Nobody Saw Coming
package.hook: You know, I almost called a competitor last month.
package.scenario: A local service business owner is having a routine catch-up with a customer he has known for four years. The customer mentions, almost as an aside, that he nearly called a competitor last month. The owner assumes it was a pricing issue or a scheduling conflict — something fixable. He asks what happened. The customer shrugs, pulls out his phone, and shows the owner his own Instagram profile. Last post: seven weeks ago. The customer explains, without any drama, that he googled the business, the website looked fine, but the social feed was completely dead. In his mind, that meant something was wrong. He almost called someone else out of genuine concern, not disloyalty. The owner stares at the screen. His business had just had its busiest quarter on record. It went quiet not because anything was wrong, but because nobody had time to post. And to a customer who could not call to check, quiet and closed look exactly the same.

video.script:
SCENE 1 — EXTERIOR, FRONT STEP OF LOCAL BUSINESS, WARM AFTERNOON LIGHT
Customer (relaxed, almost as an aside): 'You know, I almost called a competitor last month.'
Owner (confident, assumes it's routine): 'Oh yeah? What happened — pricing? Scheduling?'

SCENE 2 — CUSTOMER PULLS OUT PHONE
Customer (unbothered, matter-of-fact): 'Nah. I just figured you'd closed.'
Owner: '...Closed?'

SCENE 3 — TIGHT ON PHONE SCREEN, COOL BLUE-GREY SHIFT
Customer scrolls the owner's Instagram feed. Last post: seven weeks ago. No stories. Nothing.
Customer: 'Website looked fine. But the feed was dead. I thought something was wrong.'

SCENE 4 — WIDE ON OWNER'S EXPRESSION
Owner stares at the phone. Beat. Then quietly:
VO: 'They'd just had their busiest quarter ever. Quiet and closed look exactly the same from the outside.'

SCENE 5 — PRODUCT RESOLUTION (FENRIK STUDIO LOGO / ASSET)
Text on screen: Submit your website URL. First content package free.
VO ends. No camera. No content team. Just a URL.

product_role: fenrik Studio is introduced at the resolution as the reason this conversation never has to happen again. The owner only needs a website URL — no brief, no camera, no content team. The first package is free. The point is not to sell a service; it is to remove the only thing standing between a busy business and a consistent social presence.
narrative_arc: SITUATION: A local plumbing business owner is having a perfectly normal catch-up chat with a customer he has known for four years. The customer mentions, almost as an aside, that he nearly called a competitor last month. The owner assumes it was a pricing thing, or maybe a scheduling issue — something fixable. He asks what happened. The customer shrugs and says he just figured they had closed. The owner blinks. Closed? They had their busiest quarter on record. UNEXPECTED TURN: The customer pulls out his phone, opens Instagram, and shows the owner his own profile — the last post is from seven weeks ago. He explains, without any drama, that he googled the business, the website looked fine, but the social feed was dead. No posts, no stories, nothing. In his mind, that meant something was wrong. He almost called someone else out of genuine concern, not disloyalty. PUNCHLINE: The owner stares at the phone. His business did not go quiet because anything was wrong. It went quiet because nobody had time to post. And it turns out, to a customer who could not call to check, quiet and closed look exactly the same. CTA: fenrik Studio is introduced as the fix — submit your website URL, get your first content package free, no camera or content team required.
emotional_tone: Warm and lightly comedic — the humor comes from the absurdity of the situation, not from mocking anyone. The owner's reaction lands as instantly relatable. The customer is not upset, just honest. The punchline is a gentle gut-punch that makes the viewer laugh and wince at the same time.
audience_insight: Local service businesses, small ecommerce brands, and solo operators often treat social media as optional when they are busy — precisely when they should be most visible. They do not realize that customers use social activity as a live signal of whether a business is still operating, healthy, and worth trusting. A quiet feed does not just look boring; to a customer who cannot see behind the scenes, it looks like a closed sign.

hook: You know, I almost called a competitor last month.
scenario: A local service business owner is having a routine catch-up with a customer he has known for four years. The customer mentions, almost as an aside, that he nearly called a competitor last month. The owner assumes it was a pricing issue or a scheduling conflict — something fixable. He asks what happened. The customer shrugs, pulls out his phone, and shows the owner his own Instagram profile. Last post: seven weeks ago. The customer explains, without any drama, that he googled the business, the website looked fine, but the social feed was completely dead. In his mind, that meant something was wrong. He almost called someone else out of genuine concern, not disloyalty. The owner stares at the screen. His business had just had its busiest quarter on record. It went quiet not because anything was wrong, but because nobody had time to post. And to a customer who could not call to check, quiet and closed look exactly the same.

video.script:
SCENE 1 — EXTERIOR, FRONT STEP OF LOCAL BUSINESS, WARM AFTERNOON LIGHT
Customer (relaxed, almost as an aside): 'You know, I almost called a competitor last month.'
Owner (confident, assumes it's routine): 'Oh yeah? What happened — pricing? Scheduling?'

SCENE 2 — CUSTOMER PULLS OUT PHONE
Customer (unbothered, matter-of-fact): 'Nah. I just figured you'd closed.'
Owner: '...Closed?'

SCENE 3 — TIGHT ON PHONE SCREEN, COOL BLUE-GREY SHIFT
Customer scrolls the owner's Instagram feed. Last post: seven weeks ago. No stories. Nothing.
Customer: 'Website looked fine. But the feed was dead. I thought something was wrong.'

SCENE 4 — WIDE ON OWNER'S EXPRESSION
Owner stares at the phone. Beat. Then quietly:
VO: 'They'd just had their busiest quarter ever. Quiet and closed look exactly the same from the outside.'

SCENE 5 — PRODUCT RESOLUTION (FENRIK STUDIO LOGO / ASSET)
Text on screen: Submit your website URL. First content package free.
VO ends. No camera. No content team. Just a URL.
